title: Surface-Sensitive Mapping of Anisotropic Phonon Cascades in T$_{d}$-WTe$_{2}$
authors: Alp Akbiyik, Felix Kurtz, Sergey V. Yalunin, Claus Ropers, Hannes Böckmann
abstract: Understanding how energy flows from photoexcited carriers into the lattice is essential for describing nonequilibrium phenomena in low-symmetry quantum materials. Here, we use ultrafast low-energy electron diffraction and diffuse scattering to probe momentum-resolved phonon dynamics at the surface of T$_{d}$-WTe$_{2}$, a strongly anisotropic semimetal. Following optical excitation, the Debye-Waller suppression of Bragg peaks reveals a biexponential increase of the mean-squared atomic displacement, indicating sequential lattice relaxation. Analysis of the diffuse background reveals a preferential intensity build-up parallel to the tungsten-chain axis in the material, attributed to anisotropic electron-phonon coupling during electronic cooling. Diffuse intensity subsequently redistributes across the surface Brillouin zone and finally accumulates near the zone centre, consistent with anharmonic phonon-phonon scattering and the gradual population of low-frequency acoustic modes on a 30--100 ps timescale. The results reveal a hierarchical relaxation pathway in which energy is first deposited into selected finite-momentum phonons before spreading through the broader lattice bath. Our work highlights the importance of momentum-resolved diffuse scattering for disentangling electron-phonon and phonon-phonon relaxation in anisotropic topological semimetals.
summary: The researchers used ultrafast electron diffraction on Td-WTe2 to track how photoexcitation energy dissipates into the crystal lattice. They found that this process is not instantaneous thermalization but a multi-step cascade, first populating specific phonon modes anisotropically before spreading throughout the entire vibrational bath.
main_problem: The study aims to understand how energy deposited by photoexcited carriers flows into the lattice in low-symmetry quantum materials, specifically disentangling electron-phonon and phonon-phonon relaxation pathways.
main_result: Energy relaxation occurs via a hierarchical, momentum-selective cascade: initial rapid energy deposition into finite-momentum phonons (el-ph coupling) followed by slower redistribution across the Brillouin zone due to anharmonic phonon-phonon scattering.
method: The research utilizes ultrafast low-energy electron diffraction and diffuse scattering to probe momentum-resolved phonon dynamics at the material surface.
model_or_system: The system studied is Td-WTe2, a strongly anisotropic semimetal with broken inversion symmetry. The analysis probes its lattice response following optical excitation using ULEED techniques.
key_observables: Mean-squared atomic displacement (from Debye-Waller suppression) and the time evolution of diffuse background intensity across specific directions in the surface Brillouin zone ($ ar{\Gamma}- ar{X}$, $ ar{\Gamma}- ar{Y}$).
important_parameters: Time scales include rapid initial relaxation ($3.5 	ext{ ps}$) followed by slower lattice cooling ($30	ext{-}100 	ext{ ps}$); the anisotropy of energy flow is key.
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on separating contributions based on fluence dependence to distinguish between electronic and purely vibrational relaxation mechanisms.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate ULEED setups, biexponential fits for MSD, and momentum-resolved diffuse intensity tracking showing anisotropic build-up followed by zone center accumulation.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the need to study non-equilibrium energy flow in low-symmetry materials. It then details the use of ultrafast electron diffraction to measure time-dependent lattice dynamics, presenting evidence for sequential relaxation pathways governed by momentum conservation and anisotropy.
why_interesting: This work provides a detailed experimental blueprint for observing energy dissipation mechanisms (el-ph vs ph-ph) in anisotropic solids using advanced scattering techniques, which is highly relevant for understanding open quantum systems coupled to structured environments.
